title: TheStradman bought his burned Gallardo back from his insurer and is rebuilding the car that started his channel
dek: The orange Gallardo he owned for 11 years caught fire on a Utah road in June; the insurer totaled it, and he took it back on a salvage title to fix himself.

car.trim: Coupe; 2006 as reported by Motoring Chronicle, other reports don't give the year

source.where: Bought back directly from his own insurer after it declared the car a total loss, avoiding a salvage auction (as reported)
source.boughtNote: Not known. The insurer paid market value and he bought the car back, but neither the payout nor the buyback price has been reported [4]. He first bought the car in Newport Beach in 2015 [4].

source.damage: Fire while driving, about five minutes from home in Utah: it started on the left side behind the door and spread to the rear tires within about two minutes before passers-by put it out with extinguishers [2][3]. Burnt wiring harnesses, melted hoses, destroyed electrical connectors, damaged cooling parts and melted bodywork; the interior was almost untouched [3][4]. The worst damage centred on the EVAP canister; the cause is unconfirmed [4].

time: The fire was in mid-June 2026 (video posted June 14); the rebuild episode followed on August 5 and the insurance follow-up on October 15. About four and a half months so far; no shop hours given.

costs.note: Nothing is known yet: the insurer's payout, the buyback price and the parts bill haven't been reported. Labor is his own. We'll fill this in as the numbers are said.

value.basis: Clean-title 2006 Gallardo coupes sold for $82,500 to $130,111 from late 2025 to mid-2026 [5]. His car has over 40,000 miles and will carry a salvage, then rebuilt, title after a fire, which buyers discount heavily; our estimate for it rebuilt is $50,000 to $80,000. Its fame on his channel could pull a buyer above that.

verdict: As money, it won't pay: a fire-damaged Gallardo on a salvage title is worth less rebuilt than a clean one, and the insurer's check was the best price he'll see. As a build it makes sense for exactly one owner. This is the car that, by his account, started his channel, and he has said he fought hard to keep it. The project shows a buyback's logic: take the payout, keep the car, and the rebuild only has to be worth it to you and your viewers. The cost of the parts will decide whether it was wise.
body:
## The buy

James, the Utah YouTuber known as TheStradman, bought his Lamborghini Gallardo in Newport Beach in 2015 and put more than 40,000 miles on it over 11 years [4]. It was his first supercar and, by his own account, one of the reasons his channel took off [1][2]. Motoring Chronicle gives it as a 2006 car; the other reports don't give a year [3].

In June 2026 it caught fire. After the insurer looked at it, the car was declared a total loss: the insurer paid its market value and the car got a salvage title [4]. He then bought it back directly from the insurer rather than letting it go to a salvage auction [4]. Neither the payout nor the buyback price has been reported, so the purchase price here is unknown.

## The damage

He was about five minutes from home when he smelled fuel in the cabin, the car died and started smoking [2]. A fire started on the left side behind the door and reached the rear tires within about two minutes [2]. He had no extinguisher on board; Motoring Chronicle says he tried a bottle of Coke Zero and a car cover [3]. Passers-by stopped with extinguishers and put it out before the fire crews arrived, and his partner towed it home [2][3]. In the video posted that day he said "The OG is dead" [1].

Stripping the car showed burnt wiring harnesses, melted hoses, destroyed electrical connectors and damaged cooling parts; bodywork had melted off [3][4]. The interior was almost untouched [4]. His first suspect, a ruptured power-steering line, showed little sign of failure, and the fuel tank, filter and supply lines looked intact [4]. The worst damage was around the EVAP canister, which holds fuel vapor, and his theory is that a failure there let vapor reach a hot exhaust part or a spark. He says that is unconfirmed [4].

## The work and the parts

The rebuild began on camera in August [6]. The shopping list, as reported, is wiring harnesses, body panels and mechanical parts, and he has considered buying a damaged donor Gallardo to supply them [4]. One piece of luck: the rear bumper can be repaired rather than replaced, which he says saves thousands [4].

In October he posted "Now I Know Why Insurance Wrote off my Lamborghini" [7]. The title doesn't name the car and no outlet has reported what he found, so we've kept the episode on file without guessing at its contents.

No part prices have been given. A Gallardo harness and EVAP system aren't cheap, and the cheapest route is usually a donor car, which is why he's looking at one.

## The money

In: unknown. He got the insurer's market-value payout and paid an unreported sum to buy the car back, so his net cost is the buyback plus parts, and none of those numbers is public.

Out: clean-title 2006 Gallardo coupes have sold for $82,500 (Mecum, November 2025), $86,623 (Bring a Trailer, November 2025) and $130,111 (Bring a Trailer, July 2026, 21,000 miles) [5]. A rebuilt-title car with a fire history and over 40,000 miles is a different market: buyers discount branded titles hard, and many won't touch a fire car. We put it at $50,000 to $80,000 rebuilt. The car's fame cuts the other way: this is one of the best-known Gallardos on YouTube, and a fan could pay above that.

## What's next

Sourcing the harnesses and panels, settling the cause, and getting the car running. He has also urged viewers to keep an extinguisher in performance cars [1]. If he finds a cheap donor, the rebuild could be cheaper than the damage looks. We'll add the costs as he states them.
